description: We’re a team building Halo Health, a tool that helps astronauts track their own health on long missions and see how changes connect to conditions in the spacecraft, like CO₂, noise or temperature. We’re interested in space medicine and clear, interactive design, and our skills span UI/UX design, prototyping, research and storytelling.
summary:
We developed Halo Health, an interactive self-health tool that helps astronauts monitor and act on their own health during long-duration missions. Crew log quick daily check-ins on indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, body temperature and mood, and see them as color-coded statuses and dynamic trend charts.

What sets Halo Health apart is that it links changes in an astronaut’s health to the spacecraft environment. When sleep drops or headaches rise, it points to likely causes such as CO₂, noise, temperature or light. It shows where on the spacecraft map the problem may be, and suggests a simple test or action. It never claims causation, and it flags when a result needs a flight surgeon’s attention.

This matters because on missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean astronauts must spot problems themselves. By giving them clear, plain-language guidance, Halo Health helps crews prevent small issues from becoming critical ones. All crew health data in the prototype is simulated.
details:
What it does and how it works
Halo Health is an interactive self-health tool for astronauts on long-duration missions. Each day, crew complete a quick check-in covering indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, sleep hours, body temperature and mood. Halo Health turns these into color-coded statuses and dynamic trend charts, so an astronaut can see at a glance what is normal, what is drifting and what needs attention.

What makes it different is that it connects personal health to the spacecraft itself. Halo Health compares an astronaut’s health changes with cabin telemetry such as CO₂, temperature, noise, humidity and light. When it notices a pattern, such as poor sleep on nights when CO₂ is high, it points to the likely cause and shows where it is on an interactive spacecraft map. It then suggests a simple way to test the link and a practical action to take. It never claims a definite cause, and it flags when a result should go to a flight surgeon on the ground.

Benefits

  • Helps astronauts spot health changes early, without needing medical expertise.
  • Explains each indicator and risk in plain language, with simple instructions.
  • Turns data into clear next steps rather than just numbers.
  • Keeps flight surgeons in the loop for anything serious.

Intended impact
On missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean crews can’t rely on real-time help from Earth. Halo Health aims to give astronauts the confidence and tools to monitor themselves, catch small issues before they become critical, and fix environmental causes that may affect the whole crew. The same approach could support people in other isolated, enclosed settings, such as polar stations or submarines.

Tools and technologies
We designed the prototype in Figma and Figma Make, and built it with React and TypeScript, using Vite as the build tool and HTML and CSS for the interface, including an interactive 3D spacecraft view. We used Claude by Anthropic as an AI assistant for coding, writing and producing our demo video. Our research drew on NASA’s Human Research Program and partner space agency resources. All crew health data in the prototype is simulated and clearly labelled.

Creativity
Most health tools look only at the body. Halo Health treats the astronaut and their environment as one system and asks why a change is happening, not just what changed. Its interactive spacecraft map, its “find the likely cause, test it, act on it” approach, and its glance-first design make complex data feel like solving a clue rather than reading a medical report.

Factors we considered

  • The five hazards of spaceflight: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, altered gravity and a hostile closed environment.
  • Which measurements can realistically be taken in space, and when a result should involve a flight surgeon.
  • Clarity under pressure: astronauts are busy and not medical experts, so each screen leads with one summary and one action.
  • Scientific honesty: we show likely links, not causation, and label all simulated data.
  • Accessibility and consistency: color coding with text labels, simple language and a consistent layout across every screen.
